problem: Every layer built so far — hardware, OS, networking, identity, and enterprise services — has quietly assumed that data stays private, stays accurate, and stays reachable. Layer 6, Security, is where that assumption finally gets examined directly instead of taken for granted. The CIA Triad is the starting point because it is the simplest possible language for describing what 'secure' actually means: without it, 'security' becomes a vague feeling rather than something you can design for, measure, or argue trade-offs about.

At FundedNext, this is not abstract. The CEx application handles KYC documents, refund amounts, and ethics- related email content — three different categories of sensitive information, each with a different failure mode. If a KYC document leaks, that's a confidentiality failure. If a refund amount is silently altered by a bug, that's an integrity failure. If the tool goes down during a high-volume support day, that's an availability failure. The business problem the CIA Triad solves is giving every design decision — from who can see a sheet, to whether a formula could silently miscalculate, to how the app behaves under load — a name for exactly which kind of failure it's trying to prevent.

Cost of not doing it: without a shared vocabulary for what security even means, teams end up either securing everything indiscriminately (expensive, slow, and still incomplete) or securing nothing coherently (reactive, incident-driven, and blind to entire categories of risk like data integrity, which gets far less attention than confidentiality in most informal setups).
concept: The CIA Triad names the three core properties that security exists to protect: Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability. Nearly every security control, policy, or incident can be mapped back to which of these three properties it protects or violates, which is why the triad — despite being decades old — remains the foundational model taught in every security certification and used in every risk assessment.

Confidentiality: ensuring information is accessible only to those authorized to see it. This is the property most people think of first when they hear 'security,' and it is enforced through mechanisms already covered in Layer 4 — authentication, authorization, encryption — plus access controls and data classification still to come.

Integrity: ensuring information is accurate, complete, and has not been altered in an unauthorized or undetected way — whether by an attacker, a bug, or a well-meaning but mistaken user. Integrity is frequently the least visible of the three properties, because a silent, incorrect change often looks identical to a correct one until someone notices the discrepancy, sometimes much later.

Availability: ensuring information and systems are accessible to authorized users when they need them. This is the property most directly connected to everything covered in Sessions 79–82 (High Availability, Disaster Recovery, Monitoring, Logging) — those sessions exist largely in service of availability, even though they weren't framed as 'security' topics at the time.

A useful shorthand: confidentiality is about who can read it, integrity is about whether it's true, and availability is about whether it's there when you need it. Real incidents rarely violate just one — a ransomware attack, for instance, typically destroys availability (systems locked), threatens confidentiality (data exfiltrated before encryption), and can even threaten integrity (partial or corrupted encryption of files).
deep: Confidentiality mechanisms Confidentiality is enforced through a layered combination of authentication (proving who you are, Sessions 51–55), authorization (what you're allowed to do once authenticated, Session 60 Group Policy and beyond), encryption at rest and in transit (Sessions 46–47, IPSec and SSL/TLS), and data classification (labeling data by sensitivity so controls can be applied proportionally — public, internal, confidential, restricted). The failure mode is disclosure:
data reaching someone who should never have seen it, whether through a breach, misconfiguration, or simple oversharing of access.

Integrity mechanisms Integrity is enforced through hashing (a cryptographic fingerprint that changes if even one bit of data changes, letting you detect tampering), digital signatures (proving both integrity and authenticity of origin, tying back to PKI in Session 61), access controls that prevent unauthorized writes (not just unauthorized reads), version control and audit logging (Session 82, enterprise logging — knowing exactly what changed, when, and by whom), and input validation (preventing malformed or malicious data from corrupting a system in the first place). The failure mode is unauthorized or undetected modification — data that is wrong, but nobody realizes it yet.

Availability mechanisms Availability is enforced through redundancy and failover (Session 79, High Availability), backup and recovery (Sessions 78 and 80), capacity planning and load balancing (Session 48), and monitoring that detects degradation before it becomes an outage (Session 81). The failure mode is denial — legitimate users unable to reach a system or its data, whether from an attack (DDoS), a hardware failure, or simple overload.

The inevitable trade-offs The three properties are frequently in tension, not automatically aligned. Maximizing confidentiality (strict access controls, mandatory approval steps) can reduce availability (legitimate users delayed or locked out). Maximizing availability (broad access, minimal friction) can reduce confidentiality. Strong integrity controls (mandatory review before any change) can slow down the very availability a fast-moving support team needs. Good security design isn't maximizing all three blindly — it's choosing, deliberately and explicitly, the right balance for the specific data and system in question.
workflow: Applying the CIA Triad in practice follows a repeatable workflow used in risk assessments and security reviews across the industry:
Identify the asset — the specific system, dataset, or process being evaluated (e.g., the KYC document store within the CEx application).
Classify the asset — assign a sensitivity/criticality level, which determines how much protection is proportionate.

Assess each property separately — ask explicitly: what happens if this loses confidentiality? What happens if this loses integrity? What happens if this loses availability? Each answer is often a different scenario with a different severity.
Identify existing controls — for each property, what is currently protecting it (if anything)?
Identify gaps — where is a property under-protected relative to the impact of losing it?
Prioritize by impact and likelihood — not every gap deserves equal urgency; a low-likelihood, low-impact integrity gap can wait, while a high-impact confidentiality gap on KYC data cannot.
Select and implement proportionate controls — matching the strength of the control to the actual risk, not applying maximum security everywhere by default.
Revisit periodically — the same asset's risk profile changes as the system, its users, and the threat landscape evolve.

This workflow is exactly what a mature security review of the CEx application would look like, and it's a natural next step after the observability groundwork laid in Sessions 81–82 — you cannot meaningfully assess availability risk, for instance, without the monitoring data that reveals how the system actually behaves under stress.
enterprise: The CIA Triad sits conceptually above every layer already covered, functioning less like a single technology and more like the lens through which every other layer's controls get justified. A firewall rule, an AD group membership, a backup schedule, and a TLS certificate are all, at bottom, implementations of confidentiality, integrity, or availability — the triad is the 'why' behind decisions made throughout Layers 1–5.

Organizationally, responsibility for the triad is distributed rather than owned by a single team: a CISO or security team typically sets policy and risk tolerance, but individual system owners (network engineers ensuring availability, database administrators ensuring integrity, identity teams ensuring confidentiality) implement the actual controls day to day. Security review boards or risk committees periodically assess whether the balance across all three properties still matches business need.

At FundedNext: the CEx team is, in effect, the system owner for the Apps Script application even without a formal security title — every access decision (who can open which sheet), every validation rule in Code.gs, and every design choice about redundancy or backup is implicitly a CIA Triad decision already, whether or not it has been named as such until now.
dependencies: The CIA Triad as a concept has no technical dependencies — it's a framework, not a system — but every practical control that implements it depends on layers already covered:
Identity (Layer 4) — nearly all confidentiality and much of integrity enforcement depends on reliable authentication and authorization already being in place.
Networking and encryption (Sessions 46–47) — confidentiality in transit depends on TLS/IPSec being correctly deployed.

Monitoring and Logging (Sessions 81–82) — availability and integrity both depend on being able to detect degradation or unauthorized change in the first place; you cannot protect a property you cannot observe.
Backup, HA, and DR (Sessions 78–80) — availability specifically depends on these mechanisms already existing and being tested.
dependents: Nearly all of Layer 6, and much of what follows, is a direct elaboration of one or more triad properties:
AAA (Session 84) — Authentication and Authorization map directly onto confidentiality; Accounting maps onto integrity (a trustworthy record of who did what).
Least Privilege and Defense in Depth (Sessions 85–86) — both are strategies primarily in service of confidentiality and integrity.
Firewalls, IDS, IPS (Sessions 88–90) — primarily confidentiality and availability controls, preventing unauthorized access and disruptive attacks.
SIEM and Security Monitoring (Sessions 92, 102) — direct extensions of Session 81–82's monitoring/logging concepts, now explicitly framed around detecting violations of all three properties.

Incident Response and Forensics (Sessions 100–101) — the entire discipline of responding to and investigating a security incident is organized around identifying which triad properties were violated and to what extent.
security: This section is somewhat recursive: since the entire session is about security, but it's worth being explicit about a meta-point: the triad itself is a target for manipulation. An attacker who understands that availability failures get faster response than confidentiality failures may deliberately cause a loud, visible outage as a distraction while quietly exfiltrating data — a real, documented pattern. Treating the three properties as independent, equally monitored concerns (rather than assuming a loud availability incident is 'the whole story') is itself a security practice.

Common blind spot: organizations systematically overinvest in confidentiality (access controls, encryption) relative to integrity, because confidentiality failures (breaches) make headlines while integrity failures (quietly wrong data) often go unnoticed for a long time or are mistaken for ordinary bugs. A deliberate CIA-Triad-based review is one of the few practices that reliably surfaces this imbalance.

For FundedNext specifically: KYC data is overwhelmingly a confidentiality concern, refund calculations are overwhelmingly an integrity concern, and the support tool's uptime during peak hours is overwhelmingly an availability concern — treating all three as 'just security' without distinguishing them risks over-protecting the one that's easy to picture (confidentiality) while under-protecting the ones that are harder to picture (integrity, availability).
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Triad Failure First Check Data was viewed or shared by someone who shouldn't have access Confidentiality Review access controls, sharing settings, and authentication logs for the resource A report or calculation shows a value that turns out to be wrong Integrity Check for unauthorized or unlogged changes, validation gaps, or a bug altering data silently System or data is unreachable when a legitimate user needs it Availability Check for outage, capacity exhaustion, or a denial-of-service condition;

correlate with monitoring from Session Users report the app is 'showing old data' after an edit Integrity (or availability of the update path) Confirm whether the write actually succeeded and was logged, versus a caching or sync issue An incident seems to only involve downtime, but something feels off after recovery Possible hidden confidentiality/integrity issue behind an availability incident Explicitly check whether data was accessed or altered during the outage window, not just whether service was restored The most valuable troubleshooting habit the triad teaches is to ask all three questions every time, even when the obvious symptom clearly points to just one — many real incidents turn out to be more than one property compromised at once.
example: Consider a healthcare provider's patient portal that suffers what initially looks like a routine outage during a scheduled maintenance window. The on-call team initially treats it purely as an availability incident — restore service, move on. A later audit reveals that during the outage window, a misconfigured failover briefly routed some requests to a non-production environment with stale, unencrypted data, meaning the incident was simultaneously an availability failure and a confidentiality failure that would have gone unnoticed without deliberately checking all three properties, not just the one that was visibly broken.

The FundedNext parallel is direct: if the CEx Apps Script application ever experiences a slow period or partial failure (an availability symptom), the same discipline applies — explicitly check whether any KYC or refund data was exposed, cached insecurely, or written incorrectly during that window, rather than treating 'the tool is slow' as a purely availability-only story just because that's the symptom agents happen to notice and report first.
cloud: Cloud providers organize much of their security tooling explicitly around the triad, even when not named directly:

IAM (Session 123, upcoming) is fundamentally a confidentiality and integrity control (who can read, who can write), cloud-native DDoS protection and multi-region redundancy are availability controls, and cloud logging/audit trails (extending Session 82) are integrity controls, proving what changed and by whom.

The shared responsibility model — a concept central to every cloud provider's security documentation — is itself a CIA-Triad allocation exercise: the provider guarantees availability and confidentiality/integrity of the underlying platform, while the customer remains responsible for confidentiality and integrity of their own data and configuration on top of it (who they grant access to, how they configure encryption, whether they validate their own inputs). Misunderstanding this split — assuming the cloud provider handles more of the triad than they contractually do — is one of the most common causes of real-world cloud breaches.
automation: The CIA Triad gives a concrete lens for prioritizing which automation to build next for the CEx application, directly extending the monitoring and logging work from Sessions 81–82:

Confidentiality automation — a scheduled script that audits Google Sheet sharing settings on the underlying KYC and refund sheets and flags any unexpected 'anyone with the link' or overly broad sharing, since manual sharing-settings drift is a common, quiet confidentiality failure.

Integrity automation — input validation functions in Code.gs that reject or flag malformed refund amounts or KYC entries before they're written, plus a scheduled reconciliation check comparing a sample of stored values against an expected format or range.

Availability automation — directly reusing Session 81's synthetic monitoring check and Session 82's logging wrapper, now explicitly framed as an availability control rather than just an operational nicety.

Framing existing and planned automation this way — 'which triad property does this protect?' — is a fast, low-cost way to spot an entire missing category of protection (most informal setups, including this one historically, lean heavily toward availability and confidentiality while integrity automation lags behind).
career: The CIA Triad is the single most universally expected security vocabulary in the industry — it appears on essentially every entry-level security certification, is assumed knowledge in security-adjacent interviews at every level, and is the model hiring managers expect a candidate to reach for instinctively when asked 'how would you think about securing X.'

For someone moving from CEx support toward more technical or security-adjacent roles, being able to walk through a real system (the Apps Script application) and cleanly separate its confidentiality risks, integrity risks, and availability risks — with concrete examples of each — is a strong, structured way to demonstrate security thinking in an interview, well beyond reciting the definition.

Certification relevance: the CIA Triad is foundational material in Security+, CISSP, CISM, and virtually every cloud security certification; it is very often literally the first concept taught in each of these, underlining how central it is to the field's shared vocabulary.

misconceptions: "Security just means keeping data private": this conflates security with confidentiality alone; integrity and availability are equally legitimate security concerns, and many serious incidents are primarily about one of those two, not confidentiality at all.

"The three properties are independent of each other": in practice they're frequently in tension — maximizing one often costs you some of another, and good design is an explicit trade-off, not a pursuit of maximizing all three simultaneously.

"An outage is 'just' an availability issue": as the Real Enterprise Example shows, an availability incident can mask or coincide with confidentiality or integrity failures that go unchecked if nobody explicitly looks.

"Integrity only matters for attacks, not bugs": an unvalidated input causing silently wrong data is an integrity failure regardless of whether the cause was malicious or accidental — the triad doesn't require an attacker to be relevant.
"Small internal tools don't need to think about the triad": the CEx application handles KYC and financial data;
scale doesn't exempt a system from having real confidentiality, integrity, and availability requirements, only from needing enterprise-grade tooling to meet them.
anchors: Confidentiality = who can read it. Integrity = is it true. Availability = is it there when needed.

A ransomware attack usually hits all three at once — locked (availability), exfiltrated (confidentiality), sometimes corrupted (integrity) — the triad rarely fails in isolation during a real incident.
Confidentiality failures make headlines; integrity failures make quiet, wrong numbers that nobody double- checks — the less visible one is often the more under-protected one.
Every control you've learned so far (firewalls, backups, TLS, logging) is really just an implementation of one or more triad properties wearing a more specific name.
When investigating any incident, ask all three questions — who could have seen it, could it have been changed, was it reachable — even when only one seems obviously broken.

lab: This lab is a structured thought-and-documentation exercise rather than a technical build, since the CIA Triad is a framework applied to systems rather than a piece of infrastructure to install — but it produces a real artifact directly usable at FundedNext.
Step 1 — List the three or four most sensitive assets within the CEx Apps Script application (e.g., KYC documents sheet, refund amounts sheet, ethics email analysis data, scorecard data).

Step 2 — For each asset, write one sentence describing the realistic worst-case scenario for a confidentiality failure, one for an integrity failure, and one for an availability failure — forcing three distinct answers per asset rather than one vague 'this would be bad.'

Step 3 — For each of those scenarios, list what control (if any) currently exists today. Be honest where the answer is 'none' — this step is meant to surface real gaps, particularly around integrity, which is the property most often unprotected in informal systems.
Step 4 — Rank the resulting gaps by a rough impact × likelihood estimate, and pick the single highest- priority gap.

Step 5 — For that one highest-priority gap, design (on paper, or as a small Code.gs prototype if it's the integrity or availability category) one concrete, proportionate control — not a maximal solution, a right- sized one — and note what triad property it protects.

Completing this lab produces a lightweight, real risk assessment of the actual production application, using the exact workflow described in Section 4, and gives a concrete artifact to reference when this material comes up in a future interview.
